title: Altitude and colour
subtitle: Why high vineyards make dark wines
objectives: Explain how ultraviolet light affects skins

steps.title: Cooler with height
steps.body: Air cools by about 0.6 degrees for every 100 m of altitude. Mendoza's vineyards lie from about 700 to 1,500 m; in Salta, some reach 3,000 m. Higher sites have cooler nights, so grapes keep acidity and aroma while still ripening in strong daytime sun.

steps.title: Ultraviolet light
steps.body: At altitude, the atmosphere is thinner, and ultraviolet radiation is stronger, rising by roughly 10% for every 1,000 m. Grapes respond by producing more anthocyanins and tannins in their skins, as a natural sunscreen. Skins thicken. That's why high-altitude Malbec is so deeply coloured and structured.

steps.prompt: Why does high-altitude Malbec have deeper colour?
options: Stronger UV light makes skins produce more pigment
steps.explanation: Grapes protect themselves from UV by producing more anthocyanins, the pigments that colour wine.

steps.title: The style it gives
steps.body: The combination of strong light, cool nights and dry air gives Malbec its signature: dark colour, ripe fruit, fresh acidity and fine tannins. In the Valle de Uco, sites like Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira, at 1,100 to 1,500 m, now have their own geographical indications for this reason.

steps.prompt: Which are effects of altitude on Malbec?
steps.explanation: Mendoza is dry at every altitude; rain doesn't increase much with height there.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees per 100 m
Stronger UV thickens skins and deepens colour
Cool nights keep acidity, giving dark yet fresh Malbec
